blocks.content: Jharkhand's culture chapter is dominated by its distinctive tribal festival calendar — closely tied to the agricultural and seasonal cycle — alongside its traditional performance arts and crafts.

cells: Munda, Oraon and other tribes; spring (around Chaitra month)
Nature-worship festival marking the flowering of the Sal tree, considered sacred; among the most significant tribal festivals of the state, celebrating the new agricultural year
Santhal and other tribes; post-harvest, around Kartik/Diwali period
Cattle festival celebrating the harvest, involving decorative wall painting ('Sohrai art', see below) and cattle worship
Widely celebrated across Jharkhand's tribal and non-tribal communities; monsoon season
Festival worshipping the Karam tree/deity for prosperity and good harvest, involving distinctive Karma dance performances
Particularly in the Kurmi and other communities of the Chota Nagpur region; around Makar Sankranti (mid-January)
Harvest festival marking the end of the agricultural cycle

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Sarhul (Sal tree flowering festival) and Karma (Karam tree/deity worship) are the two most frequently tested named tribal festivals of Jharkhand — remember Sarhul marks SPRING/new year, while Karma is a MONSOON-season festival.

items: Sohrai and Khovar painting — traditional wall-art forms practised particularly around the Hazaribagh region, using natural pigments to create distinctive geometric and nature-inspired designs on mud walls during the Sohrai festival (harvest) and Khovar (marriage season) respectively; these art forms have received Geographical Indication (GI) tag recognition and growing national/international recognition as a distinctive Jharkhand folk-art tradition.
Paitkar painting — a traditional scroll-painting art form of the Santhal Pargana region, historically used by wandering picture-showmen to narrate mythological and folk stories.

Bamboo and cane craft, and Dokra metal-casting (a traditional lost-wax metal-casting technique producing distinctive tribal figurines and artefacts, also found in parts of neighbouring West Bengal and Odisha) are other significant traditional craft forms.

Chhau dance — a semi-classical, masked dance-drama form with martial-art-influenced movements, found in a shared tradition across Jharkhand (particularly the Seraikella style, named for the Seraikela area), West Bengal (Purulia style) and Odisha (Mayurbhanj style) — recognised by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Jhumar and Domkach are among the traditional folk-dance forms associated with harvest and marriage celebrations respectively across various communities of the state.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Chhau dance has THREE regional styles — Seraikella (Jharkhand), Purulia (West Bengal), and Mayurbhanj (Odisha) — and is UNESCO-recognised as Intangible Cultural Heritage; remembering all three states' style names together is a frequently tested cross-state culture fact.

items: Sarhul (spring, Sal tree worship) and Karma (monsoon, Karam tree/deity worship) are Jharkhand's most prominent tribal festivals.
Sohrai and Khovar wall paintings (Hazaribagh region) hold GI tag recognition.
Paitkar painting (Santhal Pargana) = traditional scroll-painting art form.
Chhau dance (Seraikella style in Jharkhand, alongside Purulia in WB and Mayurbhanj in Odisha) is UNESCO-recognised Intangible Cultural Heritage.
